entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Piye (reigned c. 744–714 BC) was the formidable Kushite pharaoh who founded Egypt's Twenty-fifth Dynasty, initiating a century of Nubian rule over a reunited Egypt. Ascending from his capital at Napata, deep in modern-day Sudan, Piye masterfully consolidated control over Upper Egypt before launching a decisive military campaign to subjugate the fragmented Delta kingdoms, effectively re-establishing a unified Egyptian state after centuries of political disarray. His reign marked a pivotal moment, reasserting traditional Egyptian religious and political ideals while simultaneously integrating Kushite cultural elements, profoundly impacting the Nile Valley's geopolitical landscape and religious practices.

Piye's most celebrated achievement was his "Conquest of Egypt," meticulously documented in the monumental Victory Stela, erected at the Temple of Amun at Gebel Barkal. This hieroglyphic inscription details his swift military campaign around 730 BC, where he systematically defeated a coalition of Lower Egyptian princes, including Tefnakht of Sais, Nimlot of Hermopolis, and Peftjauawybast of Herakleopolis. His strategy involved both direct military engagement and psychological warfare, leveraging his piety towards the god Amun and portraying himself as the divinely appointed restorer of Ma'at (cosmic order). After securing Memphis, he received the submission of the Delta rulers, who then paid homage and swore fealty, though he allowed them to retain local authority under his ultimate suzerainty.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Piye reunified Egypt after centuries of fragmentation, establishing the Twenty-fifth Dynasty and initiating a period of Kushite rule that revived ancient Egyptian traditions and temporarily resisted Assyrian expansion. His reign reshaped the geopolitical and cultural landscape of the Nile Valley for over a century.
